title: Nuxt 4.5: Experimental SSR Streaming, Vite 8 and an Rsbuild-Powered Rspack Builder
gist: Nuxt 4.5 -- called its 'biggest release in a while' -- ships experimental SSR streaming for faster Time to First Byte, moves to Vite 8 and an Rsbuild-powered Rspack 2 builder, and lays groundwork for Nuxt 5, but community feedback flags that streaming can create middleware/cookie correctness bugs and does not reduce actual server compute time, only perceived load time.

themes.theme: SSR streaming: real UX win, new correctness risk

insights.claim: Nuxt 4.5's headline feature, experimental SSR streaming, improves Time to First Byte by flushing the HTML shell immediately and streaming the body as Vue renders it, enabled via a single ssrStreaming config flag, with streaming automatically disabled for bots/crawlers and for routes using redirect, cache, isr, or swr rules.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A low-friction perceived-performance lever for existing Nuxt apps, but the automatic fallback list (redirects, caching rules) means the benefit won't apply uniformly across a site's routes -- teams should audit which routes actually get the TTFB improvement before claiming a blanket win.
insights.locator: The headline feature is experimental SSR streaming

insights.claim: A developer on daily.dev warned that once the HTML shell is flushed under SSR streaming, late status, header, or cookie mutations can no longer reach the client, turning middleware assumptions from a performance nuance into a correctness bug.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Teams adopting SSR streaming must audit all middleware that sets cookies/headers/status codes after initial render logic runs -- this is a hidden migration cost that could cause silent auth/session bugs in production if not caught in testing.
insights.quote: once the shell is flushed, late status, header, or cookie mutations can’t reach the client, so middleware assumptions become a correctness issue rather than only a performance concern.

insights.claim: A dev.to commenter clarified that SSR streaming does not shrink the underlying server-side render work (cited as 2.5 seconds in one example) -- it only changes what the browser can paint while that work still runs in the background.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Corrects a likely marketing misconception: SSR streaming is a perceived-latency/UX optimization, not a server-cost or compute-time reduction -- backend scaling and infra cost planning should not assume streaming reduces actual compute load.
insights.quote: streaming does not shrink the 2.5s server work. it only changes what the browser can paint while that work still runs
insights.locator: Writing on dev.to the author noted

insights.claim: Nuxt's SSR streaming is explicitly framed as following the same architectural shift React made earlier with Suspense-based streaming server rendering, with one commentator describing Nuxt as 'catching up' to React.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Signals continued cross-framework convergence on streaming SSR as the default rendering paradigm across the JS ecosystem (React, and now Vue/Nuxt) -- a maturing pattern that other frameworks not yet supporting it (e.g., older Angular SSR) may face competitive pressure to adopt.
insights.quote: the same shift React made earlier with Suspense and streaming server rendering
insights.locator: The streaming implementation is a pattern seen elsewhere with React

themes.theme: Build-tooling churn: Vite 8 and Rsbuild-powered Rspack

insights.claim: Nuxt 4.5 moves to Vite 8 and introduces an Rspack 2 builder rebuilt on top of Rsbuild, alongside a stable error code system and a new useLayout composable, as part of groundwork for the upcoming Nuxt 5.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: This release is explicitly transitional/groundwork-laying for Nuxt 5, so teams should read 4.5 as a preview of coming breaking changes rather than a stable long-term target; front-end tooling investment decisions should track the Rspack/Rsbuild builder maturity before betting on it over Vite for production.

insights.claim: The stable error code system, built on 'nostics', gives warnings a greppable code (e.g., NUXT_E1001) with a short explanation and a concrete fix to try, and a real-world example surfaced when the new built-in useLayout composable collided with Vuetify's composable of the same name, raising warning NUXT_B6002.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Naming collisions between framework-level composables and popular UI libraries (Vuetify) are a predictable friction point as Nuxt absorbs more built-in functionality; teams using Vuetify should check for useLayout conflicts before upgrading.
insights.locator: A reported issue showed the new built-in useLayout

insights.claim: In response to the useLayout/Vuetify naming collision, a Nuxt maintainer (Roe) said he was open to adding more ecosystem projects to the nuxt/ecosystem-ci test suite specifically to surface this kind of breaking-change issue before a release ships.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Signals the Nuxt team is actively expanding pre-release ecosystem compatibility testing in response to community-surfaced breakage -- a maturity signal worth watching as an indicator of fewer such collisions in future releases.
insights.locator: with Roe responding that he was happy

insights.claim: Upgrading requires refreshing the lockfile with nuxt upgrade --dedupe due to major version bumps in unhead v3 and unctx v3; the unhead v3 upgrade introduces type-narrowing for useHead that can be a breaking type change, and Nuxt 3 reaches end-of-life on July 31, 2026.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A hard deadline (Nuxt 3 EOL July 31, 2026) forces teams still on Nuxt 3 to plan migration now; the unhead v3 type-narrowing change is a concrete TypeScript breaking-change risk to budget for during upgrade testing.
insights.locator: Developers upgrading should refresh their lockfile
